newsitem.title: UK: Clarke says London Tube sell-off "possible".
newsitem.headline: Clarke says London Tube sell-off "possible".

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke on Tuesday appeared to confirm that the government may sell off London's underground railway system by referring in a speech to its "possible privatisation".
Clarke told the Centre for Policy Studies think-tank that the Conservative drive to sell off state assets had "certainly not reached the end of the road".
"There will be further privatisations in the next five years -- privatisations that will benefit the British public and keep us competitive as a nation in a tough world trading environment," he said.
Clarke said the opposition Labour party had repeatedly issued "scare stories" about the effect on service levels of every privatisation which the Conservatives had pushed through.
"The claims now being made about the possible privatisation of London Underground are precisely the same as those previously made about the railways," he said.
"In fact the 21 franchises which have so far been announced to replace British Rail have kept service at the same levels, and more than half have said they intend to increase service levels."
British newspaper reports last week suggested that ministers had delayed plans to announce a sell-off of the London Underground in a move which could raise between 600 million and 1.5 billion pounds.
But Clarke said: "As we approach the Millennium, there remains a great deal still to do to build on the success of our privatisation programme."
He mentioned only one other specific privatisation plan -- the National Air Traffic Service.
But he stressed the role that the government's Private Finance Initiative had to play in reducing public spending by getting private firms to build public infrastructure such as hospitals.

In a reponse to Clarke's speech, deputy Labour leader John Prescott accused the Conservatives of planning "a closing down sale to sell-off more public assets at knock-down prices, organised purely for party political purposes". -- London Newsroom +44 171 5427767
